warmup.why: Average latency is h × 0.5 + (1 − h) × 10: 0.595 ms at 99% and 0.5095 ms at 99.9%, about 14% lower. The database only sees the misses, and they fall from 1% of requests to 0.1%, a tenth of the load. Hit ratios hide this; miss ratios show it. The rest of the lesson builds up why caches reach ratios like these at all.

sections.h: Every step away from the CPU makes data slower to reach
sections.html:
A fraud check on a card authorization needs the merchant's profile: name, country, category code. In a HashMap inside the same JVM, that profile is at most about 100 nanoseconds away. In the database across the network, it is a millisecond or two away, more than ten thousand times further. Almost none of that time is work. It is distance: wires, kernels and queues between the CPU and the bytes.

Computers keep data in layers. Every layer further from the CPU is bigger, cheaper per byte and slower. The figure below shows the ladder, with the rungs this lesson's demo measured on my laptop in blue.

  • The CPU's own caches sit on the chip. An L1 hit takes about a nanosecond, but L1 holds only 32 to 128 KB per core on current CPUs.
  • Main memory (RAM) is a separate chip on the board. A read that misses every CPU cache takes about 100 ns.
  • A file the operating system has read recently sits in its page cache, in RAM. Reading 4 KB of it costs a system call and a copy: about a microsecond.
  • An SSD read that really goes to flash takes tens of microseconds, up to about 0.1 ms.
  • A round trip to another machine in the same data center takes something like 0.1 to 0.5 ms, before that machine does any work.
  • A round trip to another region is limited by light in glass fiber, about 200,000 km a second. Amsterdam to New York is about 5,900 km, so a round trip can't take less than about 60 ms, and real routes make 70 to 150 ms common.

Each rung costs ten to a thousand times more than the one above it. That gap is why caches exist. A cache is a smaller, faster store that keeps copies of some of the data from a bigger, slower one. A read that finds its data in the cache is a hit and pays the fast rung. A read that doesn't is a miss: it pays the slow rung, and usually leaves a copy behind for next time.

Why not copy everything up a rung? Because the fast layers are small and the data keeps changing. A server has tens or hundreds of gigabytes of RAM, and the database behind it can hold terabytes. So a cache holds only part of the data. The rest of this lesson asks which part, and what holding it is worth.

import java.nio.ByteBuffer; import java.nio.channels.FileChannel; import java.nio.file.Files; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.nio.file.StandardOpenOption; import java.util.Random; /** Measures four rungs of the latency ladder from the JVM: CPU cache, RAM, the OS page cache, a loopback round trip. */ public class LatencyDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { System.out.printf("pointer chase, 16 KB array (fits in the L1 cache): %8.1f ns per load%n", chase(16 << 10, 50_000_000)); System.out.printf("pointer chase, 4 MB array (an L2 or L3 cache): %8.1f ns per load%n", chase(4 << 20, 20_000_000)); System.out.printf("pointer chase, 256 MB array (main memory): %8.1f ns per load%n", chase(256 << 20, 10_000_000)); System.out.printf("4 KB read from a file the OS has cached: %8.1f us per read%n", cachedFileRead() / 1_000); System.out.printf("1-byte round trip over loopback TCP: %8.1f us per round trip%n", loopbackRoundTrip() / 1_000); } /** Follows a random cycle through an int array, so every load depends on the one before: no prefetching helps. */ static double chase(int bytes, int steps) { int n = bytes / 4; int[] next = new int[n]; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) next[i] = i; Random random = new Random(1); for (int i = n - 1; i > 0; i--) { // Sattolo's shuffle: one cycle through every slot int j = random.nextInt(i); int t = next[i]; next[i] = next[j]; next[j] = t; } int p = 0; for (int i = 0; i < steps / 10; i++) p = next[p]; // warm up the JIT and the caches long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < steps; i++) p = next[p]; long ns = System.nanoTime() - t0; if (p == -1) System.out.println(); // use p, so the JIT can't drop the loop return (double) ns / steps; } /** Random 4 KB reads from a 64 MB file that was just written, so every block sits in the page cache. */ static double cachedFileRead() throws IOException { Path file = Files.createTempFile("sfz-ladder", ".bin"); try { Files.write(file, new byte[64 << 20]); try (FileChannel ch = FileChannel.open(file, StandardOpenOption.READ)) { ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(4096); Random random = new Random(2); int blocks = (64 << 20) / 4096; for (int i = 0; i < 20_000; i++) { buf.clear(); ch.read(buf, (long) random.nextInt(blocks) * 4096); } int reads = 200_000; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < reads; i++) { buf.clear(); ch.read(buf, (long) random.nextInt(blocks) * 4096); } return (double) (System.nanoTime() - t0) / reads; } } finally { Files.delete(file); } } /** One byte to an echo server on the same machine and back: two trips through the kernel's network stack. */ static double loopbackRoundTrip() throws Exception { try (ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(0, 1, InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress())) { Thread echo = new Thread(() -> { try (Socket s = server.accept(); InputStream in = s.getInputStream(); OutputStream out = s.getOutputStream()) { int b; while ((b = in.read()) != -1) out.write(b); } catch (IOException ignored) { } }); echo.start(); try (Socket client = new Socket(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), server.getLocalPort())) { client.setTcpNoDelay(true); InputStream in = client.getInputStream(); OutputStream out = client.getOutputStream(); for (int i = 0; i < 5_000; i++) { out.write(1); in.read(); } int trips = 20_000; long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < trips; i++) { out.write(1); in.read(); } return (double) (System.nanoTime() - t0) / trips; } finally { echo.join(1_000); } } } }

sections.h: Requests are skewed, so a small cache catches most of them
sections.html:
If every key were equally popular, a cache would be a poor deal. Hold 10% of a million merchants and you would hit 10% of the time. Hold half and you would hit half the time. Real traffic isn't like that. A supermarket chain's merchant id shows up in thousands of authorizations a minute, and a bicycle repair shop's twice a day. Two habits of real workloads make caches pay.

The first is locality. Temporal locality means a key used now is likely to be used again soon: a customer who just paid uses the card again later that day, and a declined payment is often retried within seconds. Spatial locality means data next to what you just read is likely to be read next. CPU caches bet on it by loading 64 bytes at a time, and databases by reading whole 8 KB pages.

The second is skew: a few keys get most of the requests. A common model for it is the Zipf distribution. Rank the keys by popularity. The key of rank k gets a share of requests proportional to 1/k^α. With α = 1, the most popular key gets twice the traffic of the second and ten times that of the tenth. The exponent α says how skewed the traffic is: 0 is uniform, and bigger means more skewed. For a million merchants:

α top 0.1% of keys top 1% top 10%
0.6 6.0% of requests 15.6% 39.6%
0.8 20.7% 36.2% 60.9%
1.0 52.0% 68.0% 84.0%
1.2 82.2% 91.0% 96.5%

At α = 1, a cache that holds just 1,000 of the million merchants could answer half of all lookups.

Does real traffic look like this? Twitter's cache team collected week-long, unsampled traces from 153 of its Twemcache clusters, about 700 billion requests. In 80% of the workloads, popularity fitted a Zipf distribution well, and most α values fell between 1 and 2.5. Read-heavy workloads had a median α near 1.4 and write-heavy ones near 0.9. Production caches are often more skewed than the classic α = 1.

Skew has a second face, the long tail. In a million requests at α = 1, the demo below touched 217,407 different merchants, and 69% of them were asked for exactly once. A cache can't help a key that never comes back, and every such key takes a slot from one that will. Lesson 5 is about getting rid of those keys quickly.

code.html: package sfz.cache.l01.demo import java.util.Random import kotlin.math.pow /** How much of the traffic the most popular keys get under Zipf popularity, for four values of alpha. */ fun main() { val n = 1_000_000 // a million merchants println("alpha top 0.1% top 1% top 10% distinct keys in 1M requests seen once") for (alpha in listOf(0.6, 0.8, 1.0, 1.2)) { val cdf = cdf(n, alpha) // draw a million requests and count how many different keys they touched val random = Random(42) val seen = IntArray(n) repeat(1_000_000) { val k = cdf.binarySearch(random.nextDouble()) seen[if (k >= 0) k else -k - 1]++ // first cdf entry above the draw } val distinct = seen.count { it > 0 } val once = seen.count { it == 1 } println("%5.1f %7.1f%% %5.1f%% %6.1f%% %,28d %8.0f%%".format(alpha, 100 * cdf[n / 1000 - 1], 100 * cdf[n / 100 - 1], 100 * cdf[n / 10 - 1], distinct, 100.0 * once / distinct)) } } /** cdf[k - 1] = share of requests for keys 1..k, with key k weighted 1 / k^alpha. */ private fun cdf(n: Int, alpha: Double): DoubleArray { val total = (1..n).sumOf { it.toDouble().pow(-alpha) } var running = 0.0 val cdf = DoubleArray(n) { running += (it + 1.0).pow(-alpha) / total; running } cdf[n - 1] = 1.0 return cdf }

sections.h: Count the misses: from 90% to 99% hits is ten times better
sections.html:
The hit ratio h is the share of requests the cache answers: hits divided by all requests. The miss ratio is 1 − h. Two formulas tell you what a hit ratio is worth:

  • average latency = h × (time of a hit) + (1 − h) × (time of a miss)
  • load on the slow layer = (1 − h) × requests per second

Put numbers in. A merchant lookup takes 0.5 ms from Redis, one round trip in the data center, and 10 ms from the database. The service makes 100,000 lookups a second.

Hit ratio Average latency Database queries a second
90% 0.9 × 0.5 + 0.1 × 10 = 1.45 ms 10,000
99% 0.595 ms 1,000
99.9% 0.5095 ms 100

From 90% to 99% looks like nine points. It is ten times fewer misses, so a tenth of the database load, and the average latency falls by more than half. From 99% to 99.9% the latency hardly moves, because it is already close to the cache's own 0.5 ms, but the database load falls tenfold again. So judge a cache by its misses. "98% hits" and "2% misses" describe the same cache, and only the second tells you what the database sees.

At large scale the misses are what you build for. Meta's TAO serves more than a quadrillion queries a day, so even at a 99% hit ratio it fills its caches more than ten trillion times a day. Uber estimated that one workload of over 6 million requests a second would need about 60,000 database CPU cores without its Redis cache, against about 3,000 Redis cores with it.

One more effect hits request paths that make many lookups. If one authorization does n cache lookups, all of them hit with probability h^n. With 30 lookups at 99% that is 0.99^30, about 74%, so one authorization in four waits for at least one slow read. Meta's memcache paper describes a popular page that fetched 1,740 items at the 95th percentile. At 99.9% per item, only about 17% of those page loads would see no miss at all. This is how a cache with a great average still leaves a slow tail, the effect the Foundations track's lesson on percentiles and the tail is about.

sections.h: A miss-ratio curve says how big the cache must be
sections.html:
How big should the merchant cache be? A bigger cache misses less, but how much less depends on the traffic, so measure it.

Start with the working set: the distinct keys a workload touches in a window of time. A cache that holds the whole working set misses only on first requests. Skewed traffic has no clean edge to its working set. It has a hot core and a long tail, and each extra slot catches a little less than the one before.

To try sizes, you need a rule for what to throw out when the cache is full. The classic rule is LRU, least recently used: evict the key that has gone longest without a request. It bets that what was used recently will be used again soon, which is temporal locality turned into a rule. The stepper below runs LRU with three slots.

Now replay one recorded stream of requests through LRU caches of several sizes, and plot the miss ratio against the size. That plot is a miss-ratio curve. The demo for this section does it for a million Zipf requests over 100,000 keys:

α 100 keys 1,000 keys 10,000 keys 50,000 keys
0.8 93.2% 79.5% 53.1% 19.6%
1.0 70.9% 49.3% 26.1% 8.4%
1.2 39.3% 20.4% 8.2% 3.6%

Read the α = 1 row. A cache for 1% of the keys misses about half the requests. Ten times the memory only halves the misses again, and fifty times leaves 8%. The curve falls steeply, then flattens. So the right size depends on the miss ratio you need, and the skew decides what it costs: at α = 1.2, 10,000 slots do what 50,000 do at α = 1.

Curves can also have cliffs. A batch job that reads 1,001 keys in a loop, through a 1,000-key LRU cache, misses every single time. When key 1 comes back, LRU has just evicted it to make room for key 1,001. Give the cache one more slot and it never misses. LRU picks exactly the wrong victim here, and lesson 5 shows eviction rules that survive it.

One property makes LRU curves easy to reason about. A bigger LRU cache always holds every key a smaller one holds, so its miss ratio can never be higher. Your lab checks that, and checks the curve you measure against a formula for what LRU should do on Zipf traffic.

try.title: Draw the curve, then find the cliff
steps: Run MissRatioDemo or MissRatioDemoKt from the labs folder. For three values of α it replays a million Zipf requests over 100,000 keys through LRU caches of four sizes. Then it loops over 1,001 keys, and over 2,000 keys, with a 1,000-key cache.

code.title: MissRatioDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.cache.l01.demo; import java.util.Arrays; import java.util.LinkedHashMap; import java.util.Map; import java.util.Random; /** LRU miss-ratio curves for Zipf traffic over 100,000 keys, and the loop that defeats LRU. */ public class MissRatioDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { int n = 100_000; int[] sizes = {100, 1_000, 10_000, 50_000}; // 0.1%, 1%, 10% and 50% of the keys System.out.println("LRU miss ratio, 1,000,000 requests over 100,000 keys"); System.out.println("alpha 100 keys 1,000 keys 10,000 keys 50,000 keys"); for (double alpha : new double[] {0.8, 1.0, 1.2}) { int[] trace = zipfTrace(n, alpha, 1_000_000, 7); StringBuilder row = new StringBuilder(String.format("%5.1f", alpha)); for (int size : sizes) row.append(String.format(" %10.1f%%", 100 * lruMissRatio(trace, size, 200_000))); System.out.println(row); } for (int keys : new int[] {1_001, 2_000}) { int[] loop = new int[keys * 50]; // keys 1..n, over and over for (int i = 0; i < loop.length; i++) loop[i] = i % keys + 1; System.out.printf("loop over %,d keys: cache of 1,000 misses %.0f%%, cache of %,d misses %.0f%%%n", keys, 100 * lruMissRatio(loop, 1_000, keys), keys, 100 * lruMissRatio(loop, keys, keys)); } } /** Replays the trace through an LRU cache of {@code size} keys; the first {@code warmup} requests aren't counted. */ static double lruMissRatio(int[] trace, int size, int warmup) { Map<Integer, Boolean> lru = new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) { @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<Integer, Boolean> eldest) { return size() > size; // evict the least recently used key } }; long misses = 0; for (int i = 0; i < trace.length; i++) { if (lru.get(trace[i]) == null) { // get() also marks the key as just used lru.put(trace[i], Boolean.TRUE); if (i >= warmup) misses++; } } return (double) misses / (trace.length - warmup); } static int[] zipfTrace(int n, double alpha, int length, long seed) { double[] cdf = new double[n]; double total = 0; for (int k = 1; k <= n; k++) total += Math.pow(k, -alpha); double running = 0; for (int k = 1; k <= n; k++) { running += Math.pow(k, -alpha) / total; cdf[k - 1] = running; } cdf[n - 1] = 1.0; Random random = new Random(seed); int[] trace = new int[length]; for (int i = 0; i < length; i++) { int k = Arrays.binarySearch(cdf, random.nextDouble()); trace[i] = (k >= 0 ? k : -k - 1) + 1; } return trace; } }

try.expect: The table above is this demo's output, and both versions print the same numbers. The loop lines say loop over 1,001 keys: cache of 1,000 misses 100%, cache of 1,001 misses 0% and loop over 2,000 keys: cache of 1,000 misses 100%, cache of 2,000 misses 0%. Neither is better: once the loop is longer than the cache, LRU gets nothing at all, however much longer it is. A cache that kept any fixed 1,000 of the 2,000 keys and never evicted them would hit half the time on that loop. That gap is the opening for the policies in lesson 5.

sections.h: Caches sit at every layer, and each one is derived data
sections.html:
Follow one card authorization and count the caches it passes on the way:

Layer What it holds A hit saves you Covered in
CPU caches (L1, L2, L3) 64-byte lines of RAM a trip to RAM, about 100 ns this lesson
In-process cache (Caffeine, a ConcurrentHashMap) objects in your JVM's heap a network round trip lessons 5 and 6
Shared cache (Redis, Memcached) values by key, shared by every pod a database query this track
Database buffer pool (PostgreSQL's shared_buffers, Oracle's buffer cache) 8 KB table and index pages a disk read the Storage track's lesson on the buffer pool
OS page cache blocks of files a disk read the OS track's lesson on the page cache and fsync
CDN whole HTTP responses, near the user a trip to your data center not in this course

Some layers cache the same bytes twice. PostgreSQL reads its files through the OS, so a hot page can sit in shared_buffers and in the page cache at once. Each layer also has its own idea of what to keep, and only some of them let you choose.

Every layer in that table holds copies. The authoritative merchant profile lives in one place, the merchants table, which is its system of record. A cached profile is derived data: computed from the record, and possible to rebuild from it. The Foundations track's first lesson drew that line. Three rules follow from it, and the rest of this track keeps coming back to them.

You can lose a cache. A Redis cache that restarts empty loses no data, but every read misses until it fills again, so the database suddenly sees the full read load. Size the database for that, or warm the cache before it takes traffic (lesson 6).

A cache can be wrong. When the record changes, nobody tells the copy. A TTL (a time to live, after which the copy is thrown away) bounds how long it stays wrong, and invalidation shortens that (lessons 6 and 7).

Never keep the only copy in a cache. An idempotency key or a rate-limit counter in Redis is not a cache entry. It is the record, and it needs the settings for data, not the settings for a cache (lessons 5 and 8).

Lesson 2 asks what changes when the whole dataset lives in memory, and opens up Redis to see.

refs.title: Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition (chapter 1: systems of record and derived data)

analogy: A cache is a chef's counter. Tonight's ingredients sit within reach, everything else is in the walk-in fridge at the back, and rare spices come from a supplier across town. The chef doesn't need the whole storeroom on the counter, because most dishes use the same dozen ingredients: that's skew. When the counter is full and something new is needed, something goes back to the fridge, ideally whatever hasn't been touched for longest. The analogy breaks on copies. The onion on the counter is the onion. A cached merchant profile is a copy, and when the row in the database changes, nobody tells the copy.
world: Most reads in a payment service are cacheable: merchant profiles, BIN ranges, the day's FX rates, fraud rule settings, feature flags. They are read on every authorization and change rarely. Your services already sit on several caches: Oracle's buffer cache holds hot blocks, the Quarkus cache extension (@CacheResult, backed by Caffeine) holds objects in the heap, and Redis holds what every pod shares. A Kafka consumer that enriches each authorization event with merchant data shows the arithmetic clearly, because it handles one partition's events in order and its lookups add up. At 500 events a second, with 0.5 ms hits and 10 ms misses, a 90% hit ratio spends 0.73 seconds of every second on lookups, and 99% spends 0.30. That is the difference between a consumer that falls behind at the evening peak and one that doesn't. Watch misses per second (Caffeine's recordStats(), keyspace_misses in Redis's INFO stats), not the hit ratio alone.
mistake: The most common mistake is adding a cache without asking whether the reads are skewed, and then judging it by its hit ratio. A cache over evenly spread reads hits about as often as its share of the data: cache 10% of card tokens that are each read about once a month and you hit about 10% of the time, or less, because most of them never come back while cached. And a hit ratio near 100% hides the number that matters: 99% of 200,000 lookups a second still leaves 2,000 database queries a second, and a cold restart sends all 200,000 to the database. Before you add a cache, count requests per key in a day of logs and see how much traffic the top 1% gets. After you add it, alert on misses per second, and size the database for a cold cache or warm the cache before it takes traffic.

compare.title: An LRU map from LinkedHashMap, in Java and Kotlin

java.title: LruMap.java
java.html: // an LRU map in a few lines: access order plus a size check after every put public class LruMap<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> { private final int capacity; public LruMap(int capacity) { super(16, 0.75f, true); // true: iterate from least to most recently used this.capacity = capacity; } @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) { return size() > capacity; // called after each put: drop the LRU entry if over } } LruMap<String, MerchantProfile> profiles = new LruMap<>(10_000);

kotlin.title: LruMap.kt
kotlin.html: // an LRU map in a few lines: access order plus a size check after every put class LruMap<K, V>(private val capacity: Int) : LinkedHashMap<K, V>(16, 0.75f, true) { override fun removeEldestEntry(eldest: MutableMap.MutableEntry<K, V>): Boolean = size > capacity // called after each put: drop the LRU entry if over } val profiles = LruMap<String, MerchantProfile>(10_000)

compare.note: Both are the same JDK class: the third constructor argument, true, switches LinkedHashMap from insertion order to access order, and removeEldestEntry runs after every put. Kotlin reads size() as the property size and needs MutableMap.MutableEntry in the override's signature. Neither version is safe to share between threads. Every get moves a node in one shared linked list, so concurrent readers need a lock, and that lock is where LRU stops scaling (lesson 5). In a service, use Caffeine instead, which is concurrent and evicts better than LRU. This map is for tests, for one-thread tools and for understanding LRU.

lab.title: Generate skewed traffic, build LRU and measure its miss-ratio curve
steps: Run the tests from the labs folder. All 16 fail. None of them needs Docker: this lab is plain JVM code and the tests finish in a few seconds.

In ZipfGenerator.kt, write buildCdf, probability and next. The KDoc gives the steps. Run ./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.cache.l01.ZipfGeneratorTest' until its five tests pass. One of them checks that key 1 gets 13.36% of the traffic among 1,000 keys at α = 1.
In LruCache.java, write access. The map is built in access order, so get already moves a key to the newest end. Run LruCacheTest.

In MissRatioCurve.kt, write missRatio, measure and smallestSizeFor, then run all the tests. MissRatioCurveTest replays 300,000 Zipf requests and checks your curve against Che's approximation, a formula for LRU on this kind of traffic (see Go deeper), to within 2 points.
Read the test a loop one key bigger than the cache misses every time. Predict its two numbers before you look at the assertions.
hints: In buildCdf, keep a running sum and store it after each addition. probability(1) is cdf[0]; for any other rank it is cdf[rank - 1] - cdf[rank - 2].
For next, binary-search with lo = 0 and hi = n - 1: while lo < hi, take mid = (lo + hi) ushr 1; if cdf[mid] > u, set hi = mid, else lo = mid + 1. Return lo + 1.
entries.get(key) != null is the hit test, because every value is Boolean.TRUE. Don't use containsKey for it: it doesn't move the key.
The least recently used key is entries.keySet().iterator().next(). Remove it before you put the new key, and only when entries.size() >= capacity.
In missRatio, call cache.resetStats() after the warm-up loop, replay the rest, and return cache.missRatio().

drill.title: Write LRU's access from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Given a LinkedHashMap<K, Boolean> entries built in access order and an int capacity, write boolean access(K key): return true on a hit, and on a miss evict the least recently used key if the cache is full, then insert. Then compare. Why must the hit test use get and not containsKey?

answer.html: boolean access(K key) { if (entries.get(key) != null) return true; // get() also makes the key the newest if (entries.size() >= capacity) { K oldest = entries.keySet().iterator().next(); // access order: the first key is the LRU one entries.remove(oldest); } entries.put(key, Boolean.TRUE); // a new key starts as the newest return false; }

alt.html: fun access(key: K): Boolean { if (entries[key] != null) return true // get() also makes the key the newest if (entries.size >= capacity) { entries.remove(entries.keys.first()) // access order: the first key is the LRU one } entries[key] = true // a new key starts as the newest return false }

recap: Each layer of storage is ten to a thousand times slower than the one above it: about 1 ns for L1, 100 ns for RAM, 1 µs for a page-cache read, 0.1 to 0.5 ms for a round trip in a data center, 70 ms or more across regions.

A cache keeps copies of part of the data in a faster layer. It pays because reads are skewed: with Zipf popularity at α = 1, the top 1% of a million keys get 68% of the requests. Twitter's caches mostly had α between 1 and 2.5.
Average latency is h × hit time + (1 − h) × miss time, and the slow layer sees (1 − h) × requests. From 90% to 99% hits cuts its load tenfold, so count misses, not hits.
A request that makes n lookups sees no miss with probability h^n, which is why many-lookup requests feel the misses in their tail latency.

A miss-ratio curve, from replaying requests through caches of several sizes, says what each extra slot buys. On Zipf traffic it falls fast and then flattens; a loop just bigger than an LRU cache misses every time.
A cache holds derived data. You can lose it (and the database takes the load), it can be stale, and it must never hold the only copy of a record.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Our merchant cache hits 98% of the time, so there is nothing left to gain, and doubling its memory would be a waste." Explain what you would check before you agree.
explain.answer: 98% hits means 2% misses, and the misses are what the database and the slow requests feel. First I'd turn it into numbers. At 20,000 lookups a second, 2% is 400 database queries a second. With 0.5 ms hits and 10 ms misses the average is about 0.69 ms, while 99.5% would give about 0.55 ms and only 100 queries a second. Then I'd look at fan-out: an authorization that makes 30 lookups at 98% meets at least one miss about 45% of the time, which shows up in p95 and p99. Whether more memory helps is a question for the miss-ratio curve. I'd replay a day of real lookups through simulated caches of today's size and twice that. Skewed traffic gives a curve that flattens, so doubling might take the misses from 2% to 1.5% or to 0.5%, and only the measurement says which. Last, I'd check what the misses are. If most are first requests for keys that never come back, no amount of memory removes them.

deeper.html:
The lab checks your LRU against a formula. Che's approximation (Che, Tung and Wang, 2002) describes LRU under independent requests with one number T, the characteristic time: how many requests it takes for C distinct keys to be asked for, where C is the cache size. A key with request probability p is in the cache if it was requested within the last T requests, which happens with probability 1 − e^(−pT). Solve Σ(1 − e^(−p_i·T)) = C for T, and the hit ratio is Σ p_i·(1 − e^(−p_i·T)). For 100,000 keys at α = 1 and 1,000 slots it predicts 49.4% misses, and the demo measured 49.3%. It assumes every request is drawn independently, so it knows nothing about loops, bursts or a key that is hot for an hour and then never again.

You don't have to replay a trace once per size. Because a bigger LRU cache holds everything a smaller one holds, Mattson and colleagues at IBM showed in 1970 that one pass computes the whole curve. For each request, count how many distinct keys were used since the last request for the same key: its stack distance. A cache of size C hits exactly the requests whose stack distance is below C. Production systems sample to keep that cheap. SHARDS (Waldspurger and colleagues, FAST 2015) hashes each key and keeps only a small, fixed fraction of the keys, and still gets curves close to the full ones.

The pointer chase in the first Try used a random cycle on purpose. Walk the same 256 MB array in order and each load gets far cheaper, because the CPU fetches 64-byte lines and prefetches the next ones when it sees a pattern. That is spatial locality doing its job. The random cycle defeats both, which is why it shows the raw cost of going to RAM.

The split between systems of record and derived data opens Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 1, which counts caches, indexes and materialized views as derived data. The Storage track's lesson on materialized views built one of the others from scratch.
